Apoptosis.definition: A controlled, tidy self-destruction that a cell carries out on itself when it is damaged beyond repair or no longer needed. It dismantles the cell without spilling its contents, and it is a normal part of how a body is built and maintained.

teaches.heading: The cell cycle control system, and its three checkpoints

Asexual reproduction.definition: Reproduction from a single parent, using mitosis only, so the offspring is a genetically identical clone. Fast and cheap, but it produces no new genetic combinations.

teaches.heading: Asexual reproduction, and how many ways there are to do it

Autosome.definition: Any chromosome that is not a sex chromosome. Humans have 22 pairs of autosomes, numbered 1 to 22 in order of decreasing size.

teaches.heading: What 23 pairs actually look like

Budding.definition: Asexual reproduction in which a small outgrowth on the parent grows by mitosis into a miniature of the parent and then detaches. Hydra and yeast reproduce this way.

teaches.heading: Asexual reproduction, and how many ways there are to do it

Cell cycle.definition: The repeating sequence a cell passes through from one division to the next: interphase, in which it grows, works and copies its DNA, followed by the much shorter mitotic phase, in which it divides.

teaches.heading: The cell cycle: mitosis is the short part

Centriole.definition: A small structure that helps organise the spindle in animal cells during cell division. Plant cells build a working spindle without them.

Centromere.definition: The point at which two sister chromatids are held together, and where spindle fibres attach. You count chromosomes by counting centromeres.

teaches.heading: Seven words you cannot do this chapter without

Cervix.definition: The narrow neck at the base of the uterus, leading into the vagina. It stays almost closed, and its mucus changes across the cycle.

teaches.heading: Positive feedback: when the body wants to run away

Checkpoint.definition: A point in the cell cycle where the cell inspects a condition before it is allowed to continue. A cell that fails is held while repair is attempted and, if repair fails, destroyed by apoptosis. There are three: G1, G2 and M.

teaches.heading: The cell cycle control system, and its three checkpoints

Chromatid.definition: One half of a copied chromosome. Two sister chromatids are identical copies joined at a centromere, and they only become separate chromosomes when that centromere splits.

teaches.heading: Seven words you cannot do this chapter without

Chromatin.definition: DNA in its unwound working state — long, fine threads spread through the nucleus, too thin to see as separate objects. Genes can only be read while DNA is in this state.

teaches.heading: Seven words you cannot do this chapter without

Chromosome.definition: One long DNA molecule wound tightly around proteins so it can be seen and moved. Humans have 46 in every body cell, arranged as 23 homologous pairs.

teaches.heading: DNA, gene, chromosome — three words, one object

Clone.definition: An organism or cell genetically identical to the one it came from, produced by mitosis alone.

teaches.heading: The two definitions, and the one difference that matters

Cytokinesis.definition: The division of the cytoplasm that follows mitosis and actually produces two separate cells. Animal cells pinch inwards; plant cells build a new wall called a cell plate.

teaches.heading: The cell cycle: mitosis is the short part

Differentiation.definition: The process by which an unspecialised cell becomes a specialised one, by switching some genes on and others off. It narrows what the cell can become, and is usually one-way.

teaches.heading: Differentiation: how a cell ends up with one pattern rather than another

Diploid.definition: Having two complete sets of chromosomes, one from each parent, so the chromosomes come in homologous pairs. Written 2n. Every human body cell is diploid, with 2n = 46.

teaches.heading: Haploid, diploid, and the loop a human life runs on

Endometrium.definition: The blood-rich lining of the uterus. It thickens each cycle to receive an embryo and is shed as a period if no embryo implants.

teaches.heading: The two systems, part by part

Epididymis.definition: A tightly coiled tube on the back of each testis where sperm are stored and finish maturing. Sperm leaving the testis cannot swim properly yet; they gain that ability here.

teaches.heading: The two systems, part by part

Expressed.definition: A gene is expressed when it is being transcribed and its protein made. A gene that is switched off is still present in the DNA — it is simply not being read.

teaches.heading: Where the change comes from: birth rate and death rate

FSH.definition: Follicle-stimulating hormone, released by the pituitary gland. It drives sperm production in the testis and makes a follicle grow in the ovary.

teaches.heading: Follow the loop, then break it

Fertilisation.definition: The fusion of a sperm and an egg to form a zygote. It restores the full chromosome number, 23 + 23 = 46, and normally happens in the upper part of the oviduct.

teaches.heading: Source three: random fertilisation, and the total

Fragmentation.definition: Asexual reproduction in which the parent breaks into pieces and each piece grows into a complete organism. Common in sea anemones, starfish and corals.

teaches.heading: Asexual reproduction, and how many ways there are to do it

Gamete.definition: A sex cell — a sperm or an egg. Gametes are haploid, so that two of them can fuse without doubling the chromosome number.

teaches.heading: Four gametes, or one

Gene expression.definition: Which of a cell's genes are being transcribed at a given time. Every cell in your body has the same genes; a cell type is defined by which subset of them it keeps switched on.

teaches.heading: Gene expression: which instructions are being followed

GnRH.definition: Gonadotrophin-releasing hormone, released by the hypothalamus. It tells the pituitary gland to release FSH and LH, and it is the first step of the HPG axis.

teaches.heading: The shape of a feedback loop

HPG axis.definition: The hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal axis: the feedback loop running hypothalamus to pituitary to gonad and back, which controls sex hormone levels and gamete production.

teaches.heading: The shape of a feedback loop

Haploid.definition: Having one complete set of chromosomes — one from each pair, and no pairs at all. Written n. Human gametes are haploid, with n = 23. Haploid means one set, not half the DNA.

teaches.heading: Haploid, diploid, and the loop a human life runs on

Homologous chromosomes.definition: A matching pair of chromosomes, one inherited from each parent, carrying the same genes in the same order. They are not identical: the versions of those genes may differ.

teaches.heading: Seven words you cannot do this chapter without

Induced pluripotent stem cell.definition: An ordinary specialised adult cell that has been driven back into a pluripotent state by switching a small set of genes back on. Also called an iPS cell.

teaches.heading: Why anyone cares: stem cells and repair

Interphase.definition: The long part of the cell cycle, made of G1, S and G2, in which the cell grows, does its job and copies its DNA. It is not a resting phase — it is when almost everything happens.

teaches.heading: The cell cycle: mitosis is the short part

Karyotype.definition: A picture of all the chromosomes from one cell, arrested at metaphase and arranged in order of size with homologous partners side by side. It is used to count chromosomes and spot missing or extra ones.

teaches.heading: What 23 pairs actually look like

LH.definition: Luteinising hormone, released by the pituitary gland. It tells the testis to make testosterone, and in the ovarian cycle a surge of it triggers ovulation.

teaches.heading: Follow the loop, then break it

Meiosis.definition: The cell division that makes gametes. One round of DNA copying followed by two divisions gives four haploid cells, all genetically different from one another and from the parent cell.

teaches.heading: The three things that make meiosis different

Monosomy.definition: A karyotype with only one copy of a chromosome instead of the usual two, usually caused by nondisjunction. No autosomal monosomy is survivable in humans.

teaches.heading: Reading the result

Multipotent.definition: Able to become a limited family of related cell types. A bone marrow stem cell is multipotent: it can make any kind of blood cell, and nothing else.

teaches.heading: Stem cells, and what "potency" measures

Negative feedback.definition: A control loop in which the response acts in the opposite direction to the change that caused it, so a level is pushed back towards its set point. It is the mechanism behind almost all homeostasis.

teaches.heading: Negative feedback, and what breaks in diabetes

Nondisjunction.definition: The failure of chromosomes to separate properly during meiosis — a homologous pair at anaphase I, or sister chromatids at anaphase II. It gives gametes one chromosome too many or too few.

teaches.heading: When the shuffle goes wrong

Ovary.definition: The female gonad. It holds the immature egg cells, releases one mature egg per cycle, and produces oestrogen and progesterone.

teaches.heading: The thing this unit has to explain

Oviduct.definition: The tube carrying an egg from the ovary towards the uterus, also called the fallopian tube. Fertilisation normally happens in its upper third.

teaches.heading: The two systems, part by part

Ovulation.definition: The release of a mature egg from the ovary, triggered by the LH surge at about day 14 of the cycle.

teaches.heading: What happens when they meet

Pluripotent.definition: Able to become any cell type of the body, but not the placenta. Embryonic stem cells, from the inner cell mass of a blastocyst, are pluripotent.

teaches.heading: Stem cells, and what "potency" measures

Polar bodies.definition: The three small cells produced alongside an egg during oogenesis. Each has a full haploid set of chromosomes but almost no cytoplasm, and they break down. They are the price of giving one cell enough material to build an embryo.

teaches.heading: Four gametes, or one

Puberty.definition: The point at which the hypothalamus switches the HPG axis on, so the gonads begin making gametes and producing sex hormones in quantity for the first time.

teaches.heading: The two systems, part by part

Sex chromosomes.definition: The 23rd pair in humans. Two X chromosomes give a chromosomally female karyotype; an X and a Y give a chromosomally male one, because the Y carries the SRY gene.

teaches.heading: What 23 pairs actually look like

Sexual reproduction.definition: Reproduction in which two haploid gametes fuse at fertilisation. It is slower and costlier than asexual reproduction, and it produces offspring that are all genetically different.

teaches.heading: Sexual reproduction, and the price it pays

Spindle fibre.definition: A protein cable that grows out from one end of a dividing cell, attaches to a centromere, and shortens to pull chromosomes apart.

teaches.heading: The five stages, and what each one is for

Stem cell.definition: An unspecialised cell that can both renew itself by dividing and give rise to specialised cell types. Both halves are required — a cell that only does one of them is not a stem cell.

teaches.heading: Stem cells, and what "potency" measures

Testis.definition: The male gonad. Its coiled seminiferous tubules make sperm by meiosis, and the cells between them make testosterone.

teaches.heading: The thing this unit has to explain

Tetrad.definition: A homologous pair of chromosomes paired up in prophase I of meiosis — four chromatids lying together. Crossing over happens while they are in this arrangement.

teaches.heading: The three things that make meiosis different

Totipotent.definition: Able to become any cell type at all, including the placenta and other supporting tissues — that is, able to build a whole organism. Only the zygote and the cells of the first few divisions are totipotent.

teaches.heading: Stem cells, and what "potency" measures

Trisomy.definition: A karyotype with three copies of a chromosome instead of two, usually caused by nondisjunction. Trisomy 21 is Down syndrome.

teaches.heading: Reading the result

Tumour.definition: A mass of cells produced when cells that have lost the ability to stop dividing keep on dividing. A benign tumour stays in one place; a malignant one invades and can spread.

teaches.heading: The thing this unit has to explain

Urethra.definition: The tube running the length of the penis. In males it carries both urine and semen, at different times.

teaches.heading: Two doors out of a villus

Uterus.definition: The muscular chamber where an embryo implants and develops. Its wall is mostly smooth muscle, which is what contracts during labour.

teaches.heading: Positive feedback: when the body wants to run away

Vagina.definition: The muscular tube connecting the cervix to the outside of the body.

teaches.heading: The two systems, part by part

Vas deferens.definition: The muscular tube carrying sperm from the epididymis up and over the bladder to the urethra. It is the tube cut in a vasectomy.

teaches.heading: The two systems, part by part

Zygote.definition: The single diploid cell formed when a sperm fertilises an egg. Every cell in a body is descended from one zygote by mitosis.

teaches.heading: The thing this unit has to explain

hCG.definition: Human chorionic gonadotrophin, released by an implanted embryo. It keeps the corpus luteum alive so progesterone stays high and the uterus lining is not shed. Pregnancy tests detect it.

teaches.heading: The ovarian and menstrual cycles

Hypertonic.definition: Describing a solution with a higher solute concentration than the cell in it. There is a net movement of water out of the cell.

Hypotonic.definition: Describing a solution with a lower solute concentration than the cell in it. There is a net movement of water into the cell.

Isotonic.definition: Describing a solution with the same solute concentration as the cell in it. Water crosses in both directions at equal rates, so there is no net movement.

Hydrophilic.definition: Attracted to water. Polar molecules and ions are hydrophilic, so they dissolve in water.

teaches.heading: Membrane structure

Hydrophobic.definition: Not attracted to water. Non-polar molecules, such as fats and oils, are hydrophobic, so they do not dissolve in water.

teaches.heading: Membrane structure

Fluid mosaic model.definition: The model of a cell membrane as a phospholipid bilayer in which the phospholipids move sideways (fluid) and proteins are scattered throughout (mosaic).

teaches.heading: Membrane structure

Selectively permeable.definition: Describing a membrane that lets some substances cross and stops others. A cell membrane is selectively permeable because of its oily core and its transport proteins.

teaches.heading: Membrane structure

Passive transport.definition: The movement of substances across a membrane that needs no energy from the cell, such as diffusion and osmosis.

teaches.heading: Diffusion

Plasmolysis.definition: The shrinking of a plant cell's living contents away from its cell wall, when water leaves the cell in a hypertonic solution.

teaches.heading: Osmosis

Lysis.definition: The bursting of a cell when its membrane breaks. An animal cell can lyse in a hypotonic solution because it has no cell wall.

teaches.heading: Osmosis

Crenation.definition: The shrinking and wrinkling of an animal cell, such as a red blood cell, when water leaves it in a hypertonic solution.

teaches.heading: Osmosis

Anabolic.definition: Describes a reaction that builds large molecules from smaller ones, which needs an energy supply. Making a protein from amino acids is anabolic.

teaches.heading: Energy and matter, into and out of a body

Atmosphere.definition: The layer of air around the Earth. It is a small carbon reservoir, holding carbon mostly as carbon dioxide, and everything else passes through it.

teaches.heading: The layers, and the problem each one solves

Biosphere.definition: All living things, together with dead organic matter and soil carbon. It holds less carbon than the atmosphere does.

teaches.heading: From atom to biosphere

Bond energy.definition: The amount of energy needed to break a particular chemical bond. Breaking bonds always takes energy in; forming them always gives energy out.

teaches.heading: Where the energy in a sugar molecule actually sits

Calvin cycle.definition: The second half of photosynthesis, in the stroma. It uses ATP and NADPH to build carbon dioxide into sugar, and needs no light directly.

teaches.heading: The Calvin cycle — building carbon into sugar

Carbon sink.definition: A reservoir that takes in more carbon than it releases over a period of time. A growing forest is a carbon sink.

teaches.heading: Four spheres, sources and sinks

Carbon source.definition: A reservoir that releases more carbon than it takes in over a period of time. A burning forest is a carbon source.

teaches.heading: Four spheres, sources and sinks

Catabolic.definition: Describes a reaction that breaks large molecules into smaller ones, usually releasing energy. Digestion and respiration are catabolic.

teaches.heading: Energy and matter, into and out of a body

Cellular respiration.definition: The controlled release of energy from food molecules inside cells, to make ATP. Every living thing does it, and it is not the same as breathing.

teaches.heading: What cellular respiration is — and what it is not

Chemical bond.definition: The shared arrangement of electrons that holds two atoms together in a molecule. Every bond sits at a particular energy level.

teaches.heading: Where the energy in a sugar molecule actually sits

Chlorophyll.definition: The green pigment that absorbs light for photosynthesis. It absorbs blue and red light well and reflects green, which is why plants look green.

teaches.heading: Inside a chloroplast — and why plants are green

Chloroplast.definition: The organelle in a plant cell where photosynthesis happens. It contains stacks of thylakoid membranes surrounded by a fluid called stroma.

teaches.heading: Inside a chloroplast — and why plants are green

Consumer.definition: An organism that gets its organic molecules by eating other organisms. Herbivores are primary consumers, and things that eat herbivores are secondary consumers.

teaches.heading: The loop, and one thing the equation gets slightly wrong

Cristae.definition: The deep folds of a mitochondrion's inner membrane. Folding multiplies the membrane area, so more electron transport chains fit inside.

teaches.heading: Two ways to live with the ratio

Cuticle.definition: The thin, transparent, waxy layer coating the outside of a leaf. It stops the leaf drying out while still letting light through.

teaches.heading: The layers, and the problem each one solves

Decomposer.definition: An organism that feeds on dead organic matter, such as a fungus or a bacterium. Decomposers return the carbon in dead material to the air by respiring it.

teaches.heading: The same two processes, at the scale of a landscape

Energy.definition: The capacity to do work or transfer heat. Energy has no mass and takes up no space, so it is not a substance; you only ever see what it does.

teaches.heading: Energy and matter, into and out of a body

Energy pyramid.definition: A diagram showing the energy available at each trophic level, drawn with band widths in proportion. Roughly ten per cent passes to the level above, so the top band is tiny.

teaches.heading: Draw the pyramid — to scale

Facultative anaerobe.definition: An organism that uses oxygen when it is available and ferments when it is not. Yeast and your own muscle cells both qualify.

teaches.heading: Two ways to dump the electrons

Fermentation.definition: What a cell does when there is no oxygen. It makes no ATP itself; its job is to unload NADH so that glycolysis can keep running.

teaches.heading: What actually goes wrong when the oxygen runs out

Geosphere.definition: Earth's rock and sediment, including limestone and fossil fuels. It is by far the largest carbon store, and by far the slowest.

teaches.heading: The processes that move carbon

Glycolysis.definition: The first stage of respiration, in the cytosol. It splits glucose into two pyruvate molecules, needs no oxygen, and nets 2 ATP.

teaches.heading: Four stages, and where each one happens

Granum.definition: A stack of thylakoids inside a chloroplast. Stacking them packs a large amount of light-catching membrane into a small space.

teaches.heading: Inside a chloroplast — and why plants are green

Guard cell.definition: One of a pair of curved cells either side of a stoma. They swell and shrink to open and close the pore, trading water loss against carbon dioxide supply.

teaches.heading: The stoma, and the compromise the whole leaf is built around

Hydrosphere.definition: All of Earth's water — oceans, lakes and rivers. It holds roughly fifty times as much carbon as the atmosphere, dissolved as carbon dioxide and carbonate.

teaches.heading: Four spheres, sources and sinks

Kinetic energy.definition: Energy something has because it is moving. A running person, a moving car, and the vibrating molecules in a hot pan all have kinetic energy.

teaches.heading: Kinds of energy, and the only division that matters

Light reactions.definition: The first half of photosynthesis, in the thylakoid membranes. They capture light energy, split water, release oxygen, and make ATP and NADPH.

teaches.heading: The light reactions — what light actually does

Lower epidermis.definition: The protective layer of cells on the underside of a leaf. It is pierced by the stomata.

teaches.heading: The layers, and the problem each one solves

Matrix.definition: The fluid inside a mitochondrion's inner membrane. Pyruvate oxidation and the citric acid cycle happen there.

teaches.heading: The mitochondrion

Matter.definition: Anything that has mass and takes up space. Everything made of atoms is matter — a leaf, a lungful of air, a wolf.

teaches.heading: Energy and matter, into and out of a body

Mitochondrion.definition: The organelle where most of cellular respiration happens. Its inner membrane is folded into cristae, which carry the electron transport chain.

teaches.heading: The mitochondrion

NADH.definition: A carrier molecule that collects electrons and hydrogen from the early stages of respiration and delivers them to the electron transport chain.

teaches.heading: Four stages, and where each one happens

NADPH.definition: A carrier molecule that ferries hydrogen atoms and high-energy electrons from the light reactions to the Calvin cycle.

teaches.heading: The equation, and everything it hides

Obligate anaerobe.definition: An organism that cannot use oxygen at all and is usually poisoned by it, such as the bacteria that cause tetanus and botulism.

teaches.heading: Two ways to dump the electrons

Palisade mesophyll.definition: The tall, upright, tightly packed cells near the top of a leaf. They hold most of the chloroplasts and do most of the photosynthesis.

teaches.heading: The layers, and the problem each one solves

Phloem.definition: The tubes that carry dissolved sugar away from a leaf to wherever the rest of the plant needs it.

teaches.heading: The layers, and the problem each one solves

Photolysis.definition: The splitting of water using light energy in the thylakoid. It supplies replacement electrons and hydrogen ions, and releases oxygen as waste.

teaches.heading: Seeing stomata for yourself

Potential energy.definition: Energy something has because of where it is or how it is arranged. A diver on a high board and a charged battery both store potential energy.

teaches.heading: Kinds of energy, and the only division that matters

Spongy mesophyll.definition: The loosely packed rounded cells lower in a leaf, with large air gaps between them. The gaps let carbon dioxide diffuse quickly to every cell.

teaches.heading: The layers, and the problem each one solves

Stoma.definition: A tiny pore through the underside of a leaf, and the leaf's only doorway for gas. Carbon dioxide enters through it while oxygen and water vapour leave.

teaches.heading: The stoma, and the compromise the whole leaf is built around

Stroma.definition: The fluid filling a chloroplast around the thylakoids. It is full of enzymes, and the Calvin cycle happens in it.

teaches.heading: Inside a chloroplast — and why plants are green

Thylakoid.definition: A flattened disc of membrane inside a chloroplast. Chlorophyll sits in thylakoid membranes, and the light reactions happen there.

teaches.heading: Inside a chloroplast — and why plants are green

Trophic omnivore.definition: An animal that eats organisms from more than one trophic level, so it does not fit in a single band. Anything that eats a trophic omnivore is one too.

teaches.heading: Chains, levels, and which way the arrows point

Upper epidermis.definition: The single layer of clear, box-shaped cells just beneath a leaf's cuticle. It has almost no chloroplasts, so it acts as a window.

teaches.heading: The layers, and the problem each one solves

Vein.definition: A bundle of transport tubes running through a leaf. It carries water in through the xylem and sugar away through the phloem.

teaches.heading: Two doors out of a villus

Xylem.definition: The tubes that carry water and dissolved minerals up from a plant's roots to its leaves.

teaches.heading: The layers, and the problem each one solves

ATP.definition: The small molecule cells use as a rechargeable energy store. Reactions that release energy charge it up; reactions that need energy spend it.

teaches.heading: ATP, and where the matter went

Absorption.definition: The movement of small, digested molecules out of the gut and into the blood or lymph. This is the moment food stops being contents of a tube and becomes part of your body.

teaches.heading: Learning targets for the unit

Accuracy.definition: How close a measurement is to the true value. Repeating a measurement does not improve accuracy if something is shifting every reading the same way.

teaches.heading: Learning targets for the unit

Amino acid.definition: The monomer that proteins are built from. There are twenty, all sharing the same backbone and each carrying a different side group, and every one contains nitrogen.

teaches.heading: What you will actually do

Anabolism.definition: The half of metabolism that builds large molecules from small ones, such as making protein from amino acids. Anabolic reactions require energy.

teaches.heading: Energy and matter, into and out of a body

Aquaporin.definition: A channel protein that lets water cross a membrane quickly. Most aquaporins let almost nothing else through, including ions and sugars.

teaches.heading: Water, aquaporins, and why diarrhoea kills

Basal metabolic rate.definition: The energy a body uses simply to stay alive while completely at rest — running the heart, brain, kidneys and repair. It is usually the largest part of daily energy use, and it rises as body mass rises.

teaches.heading: Manipulating variables: diet, exercise and body mass

Bile.definition: A greenish fluid made by the liver and stored in the gall bladder. It contains no enzymes: its job is to emulsify fat, breaking large globules into tiny droplets so that lipase has more surface to work on.

teaches.heading: Why you have to do anything to food at all

Catabolism.definition: The half of metabolism that breaks large molecules into small ones, such as digesting starch into glucose. Catabolic reactions release energy.

teaches.heading: Energy and matter, into and out of a body

Causation.definition: A claim that one thing actually produces a change in another. Establishing it needs a mechanism and usually an experiment, not just data showing that two things move together.

Cell.definition: The smallest unit that can carry out all the processes of life, enclosed by a membrane that controls what enters and leaves. Every living thing is made of one or more of them.

teaches.heading: Why cells divide at all

Cell theory.definition: The idea that every living thing is made of one or more cells, that the cell is the smallest unit of life, and that every cell comes from another cell.

teaches.heading: From atom to biosphere

Chemical digestion.definition: Breaking the bonds inside large food molecules using enzymes, so that big molecules become small ones. Unlike mechanical digestion, this changes what the molecules are.

teaches.heading: Why you have to do anything to food at all

Chylomicron.definition: A droplet of digested fat wrapped in protein, made inside a villus cell. It is far too large to enter a capillary, so it leaves through the lacteal and travels in the lymph instead.

teaches.heading: Two doors out of a villus

Chyme.definition: The soupy, acidic mixture of partly digested food that the stomach produces by churning a bolus with acid and pepsin.

teaches.heading: Why you have to do anything to food at all

Control group.definition: The condition in an investigation where the independent variable is absent, used as the comparison. Another level of the independent variable is a second treatment, not a control.

teaches.heading: Using the evidence: the case of poor protein digestion

Controlled variable.definition: Anything other than the independent variable that could affect your result, deliberately held the same in every test so it cannot become a rival explanation.

Correlation.definition: A pattern in data where two things change together. It is a statement about the numbers, and on its own it never shows that one thing caused the other.

Dependent variable.definition: The thing you measure in an investigation, which you think depends on the independent variable. It goes on the vertical axis of a graph.

teaches.heading: What an investigation actually is

Egestion.definition: Getting rid of material that was never absorbed — fibre, dead gut lining and bacteria — through the anus. It is not the same as excretion, because this material was never inside a body cell.

teaches.heading: Why you have to do anything to food at all

Emergent property.definition: Something an assembled system can do that none of its parts can do alone. One intestinal cell can absorb a glucose molecule; only a whole folded sheet of them can absorb a meal.

Emulsification.definition: Breaking a large globule of fat into many tiny droplets. No chemical change happens — but the total surface area rises enormously, which is what lets lipase work quickly.

teaches.heading: Who does what: the chemical work, stated precisely

Endergonic.definition: Describes a reaction that takes energy in. Building large molecules from small ones is endergonic, which is why growth costs food.

teaches.heading: Downhill and uphill: exergonic and endergonic

Enzyme.definition: A protein that speeds up one specific chemical reaction without being used up. Its shape decides what it works on, so heat or the wrong pH can destroy it by unfolding it.

Error bar.definition: A line drawn on a graph showing how uncertain a mean is, most often one standard error either side of it. If two error bars overlap, the difference between the means is not convincing.

Essential amino acids.definition: The nine amino acids your body cannot build for itself and must get ready-made from food. The other eleven can be made from sugar plus a nitrogen atom transferred from elsewhere.

teaches.heading: Following the atoms

Excretion.definition: Getting rid of waste your own cells produced, such as urea, carbon dioxide and excess salt. It is done by the urinary system, the lungs and the skin — never by the gut.

teaches.heading: Why you have to do anything to food at all

Exergonic.definition: Describes a reaction that gives energy out. Breaking large molecules into small ones is exergonic, which is how food powers a body.

teaches.heading: Downhill and uphill: exergonic and endergonic

Fibrin.definition: The insoluble protein mesh that forms across a wound and traps blood cells to make a clot. It is made from soluble fibrinogen by the enzyme thrombin.

teaches.heading: Positive feedback: when the body wants to run away

Glucagon.definition: The hormone released by the pancreas when blood glucose falls too low. It tells the liver to break glycogen back down into glucose and release it into the blood.

teaches.heading: The five components of a feedback loop

Glycogen.definition: The storage form of glucose in animals — a branched polymer kept mainly in the liver and muscles. It is built when insulin signals plenty and broken down when glucagon signals shortage.

teaches.heading: Negative feedback, and what breaks in diabetes

Gut–brain axis.definition: The continuous two-way communication between the digestive system and the brain, carried by the vagus nerve, by hormones in the blood and by chemicals made by gut bacteria. Most of the traffic runs from gut to brain.

Hepatic portal vein.definition: The unusual vein that carries blood from the gut straight to the liver rather than back to the heart. It means the liver inspects every gram of absorbed sugar and amino acid before the rest of the body gets any.

teaches.heading: Two doors out of a villus

Homeostasis.definition: Keeping conditions inside a body steady — temperature, blood glucose, water, pH — whatever is happening outside. It is active work, not a resting state, and it is done by feedback loops.

teaches.heading: Learning targets for the unit

Hydrolysis.definition: Splitting a large molecule into smaller ones by adding water across the bond. Every digestive enzyme is doing this, and a water molecule is genuinely used up at each bond broken.

teaches.heading: Four families, one design idea

Hypothesis.definition: A testable prediction with a reason attached. A good one states a direction and commits to a mechanism, so a result that goes the other way tells you something specific.

teaches.heading: What an investigation actually is

Independent variable.definition: The one thing you deliberately change in an investigation. If there is more than one, you cannot tell which of them caused the result.

teaches.heading: What an investigation actually is

Ingestion.definition: Taking food into the digestive tube. Eating.

teaches.heading: Why you have to do anything to food at all

Insulin.definition: The hormone released by the pancreas when blood glucose rises. It is a message, not a chemical that destroys sugar: it tells liver and muscle cells to take glucose in and store it as glycogen.

teaches.heading: The five components of a feedback loop

Lacteal.definition: The lymph vessel running up the centre of every villus. It collects absorbed fat, which is too big to enter the blood capillaries beside it.

teaches.heading: Structure makes function possible

Lymphatic system.definition: A one-way drainage network that collects fluid from tissues, carries absorbed fat from the gut, and houses immune cells. It has no pump of its own and is pushed along by ordinary muscle movement.

teaches.heading: Eleven systems, one body

Macromolecule.definition: A very large molecule built from many repeated small units — a carbohydrate, a lipid, a protein or a nucleic acid.

teaches.heading: Using the evidence: the case of poor protein digestion

Mechanical digestion.definition: Physically breaking food into smaller pieces, by chewing or churning. Nothing changes chemically; what changes is the surface area available to enzymes.

teaches.heading: Why you have to do anything to food at all

Metabolism.definition: All the chemical reactions happening inside a living thing — the building reactions and the breaking-down reactions together.

teaches.heading: Learning targets for the unit

Microbiome.definition: The population of bacteria and other microorganisms living in your gut. They digest fibre you cannot, make vitamins you cannot, and crowd out harmful species.

teaches.heading: The gut is also a sense organ

Microvilli.definition: Thousands of tiny projections on the surface of every cell covering a villus. They multiply the absorbing surface again and hold the final digestive enzymes in the membrane itself.

teaches.heading: Structure makes function possible

Model.definition: A deliberately simplified stand-in for something you cannot easily observe or test directly. A model is judged by what it is for, not by how accurate it is overall — and knowing where it breaks is part of understanding it.

teaches.heading: Models: useful and wrong at the same time

Monomer.definition: The small repeating unit that a polymer is built from — a glucose molecule, an amino acid or a nucleotide.

Monosaccharide.definition: A single sugar unit, such as glucose, fructose or galactose. All three have the formula C6H12O6 and differ only in how the atoms are arranged.

teaches.heading: Four families, one design idea

Oral rehydration salts.definition: A drink of glucose and salts in clean water, used to treat severe dehydration. It works because the transporter SGLT1 carries glucose and sodium across the gut wall together, and water then follows the sodium by osmosis.

teaches.heading: The case we keep coming back to

Organ system.definition: A group of organs that co-operate on one large task, such as the digestive system or the circulatory system. No organ system in a body can complete its job without others.

teaches.heading: From atom to biosphere

Organelle.definition: A structure inside a cell that does one particular job, such as a mitochondrion or a nucleus. Despite the name, an organelle is one level below a cell, not above it.

teaches.heading: From atom to biosphere

Oxytocin.definition: The hormone released by the pituitary that makes the uterus contract during labour. It drives a positive feedback loop: contraction stretches the cervix, which releases more oxytocin.

teaches.heading: Positive feedback: when the body wants to run away

Pepsin.definition: The protein-digesting enzyme of the stomach. It works only in strong acid and it cuts within a protein chain, so what it produces is shorter chains called peptides — not single amino acids.

teaches.heading: Why you have to do anything to food at all

Polymer.definition: A long chain built from many identical or similar small units joined together.

Polysaccharide.definition: A carbohydrate made of many sugar units joined in a chain, such as starch, glycogen or cellulose.

teaches.heading: Four families, one design idea

Positive feedback.definition: A control loop in which the response makes the original change larger, so the process accelerates. It is used for jobs that must be finished quickly — clotting, vomiting, sneezing, childbirth — and each one ends by destroying its own stimulus.

teaches.heading: Positive feedback: when the body wants to run away

Precision.definition: How closely repeated measurements agree with one another. A precise measurement can still be wrong if something is biasing every reading the same way.

teaches.heading: Learning targets for the unit

Protein.definition: A macromolecule built from one or more chains of amino acids, folded into a precise shape. The shape decides the job: enzymes, insulin and the channels in a cell membrane are all proteins.

teaches.heading: Using the evidence: the case of poor protein digestion

Reliability.definition: Whether you would get the same result if the whole investigation were done again. Repeats and a clearly described method are what build it.

teaches.heading: How much data, how good, and knowing when to stop

Saturated fat.definition: A fat whose fatty acid chains carry as many hydrogen atoms as possible, with no double bonds. The chains are straight, so they pack closely together and the fat is usually solid at room temperature.

teaches.heading: Four families, one design idea

Standard error.definition: A measure of how much a mean would move if you repeated the whole investigation with a different sample. It is the standard deviation divided by the square root of the number of measurements, so it shrinks only slowly as you add repeats.

teaches.heading: Reading the data honestly

Transamination.definition: Moving an amino group from one molecule to another, which is how a cell puts nitrogen into a new amino acid. Nitrogen is passed around inside you; it is never made.

teaches.heading: Following the atoms

Unsaturated fat.definition: A fat whose fatty acid chains contain one or more double bonds between carbons. Each double bond kinks the chain, so the molecules cannot pack closely and the fat is usually liquid at room temperature.

teaches.heading: Four families, one design idea

Vasoconstriction.definition: Narrowing of the small arteries supplying the skin, which keeps warm blood away from the surface and reduces heat loss.

teaches.heading: Staying the same while everything changes

Vasodilation.definition: Widening of the small arteries supplying the skin, which brings warm blood to the surface so that heat is lost.

teaches.heading: Staying the same while everything changes

Villus.definition: A finger-shaped projection of the lining of the small intestine, about a millimetre long. Millions of them multiply the absorbing surface, and each contains a capillary network and a lacteal.

teaches.heading: Two doors out of a villus

Abiotic.definition: A non-living part of an ecosystem — temperature, rainfall, sunlight, soil, wind, fire. Abiotic factors usually act on a population regardless of how crowded it is.

teaches.heading: Two kinds of limiting factor

Binary fission.definition: The way bacteria reproduce: a cell copies its DNA and splits into two identical cells. Because every cell divides, the whole population doubles each generation.

teaches.heading: Why growth accelerates

Bioaccumulation.definition: The build-up of a substance inside a single organism over its lifetime, because it takes the substance in faster than it can get rid of it. Fat-soluble poisons like DDT do this because they cannot be flushed out in urine.

teaches.heading: Why the poison ended up in the cats

Biomagnification.definition: The increase in the concentration of a substance at each step up a food chain. A predator eats many prey animals and keeps all of their poison, so top predators end up with far higher concentrations than anything below them.

teaches.heading: Why the poison ended up in the cats

Biotic.definition: A living part of an ecosystem — the other organisms in it, including predators, prey, competitors, parasites and diseases. Biotic factors usually hit harder when a population is crowded.

teaches.heading: Two kinds of limiting factor

Birth rate.definition: The number of live births per 1,000 individuals per year. Using 'per 1,000' rather than a raw count lets you compare a small population with a huge one.

teaches.heading: Where the change comes from: birth rate and death rate

Carrying capacity.definition: The largest number of individuals of a population that an environment can support over the long term, written K. It is set by whatever resource runs out first, and it can change if conditions change.

teaches.heading: Learning targets for the unit

Climax community.definition: The relatively stable community a site settles into at the end of succession. It is stable only until the next disturbance, and it is not always the most diverse stage.

teaches.heading: Seral stages, climax communities, and an honest caveat

Community.definition: All the populations of all the different species living together in one area — every plant, animal, fungus and microbe, but not the non-living surroundings.

teaches.heading: Seral stages, climax communities, and an honest caveat

Competition.definition: Two or more organisms needing the same limited resource, such as food, water, space or light. It is one of the main density-dependent factors limiting population size.

teaches.heading: Competition, and why a web is more stable than a chain

Death rate.definition: The number of deaths per 1,000 individuals per year. When the death rate is higher than the birth rate a population shrinks.

teaches.heading: Where the change comes from: birth rate and death rate

Density-dependent.definition: A limiting factor that hits harder when a population is crowded — predation, competition, disease, and the build-up of waste. These factors act like a thermostat and are what regulate a population near its carrying capacity.

teaches.heading: Learning targets for the unit

Density-independent.definition: A limiting factor that does the same damage no matter how crowded a population is — weather, fire, floods, volcanic eruptions, pollution. These knock a population about but do not regulate it.

teaches.heading: Learning targets for the unit

Doubling time.definition: How long a population takes to double in size. For a steady growth rate you can estimate it with the rule of 70: doubling time is roughly 70 divided by the percentage growth per year.

teaches.heading: Doubling time, and the arithmetic behind it

Ecological succession.definition: The gradual, fairly predictable change in the community of species living in an area over time, after a disturbance or on newly exposed ground. Each stage changes the conditions so that the next stage can move in.

teaches.heading: Learning targets for the unit

Ecosystem.definition: A community of organisms together with the non-living things it depends on — soil, water, air and sunlight — all interacting as one system.

teaches.heading: Rebuild an ecosystem

Exponential growth.definition: Growth where the number added is proportional to the number already there, so growth accelerates. It draws a J-shaped curve, and it looks almost flat for a long time before it takes off.

teaches.heading: What you will actually do

Food chain.definition: A single line showing who eats whom, such as grass to mouse to snake to hawk. It is a simplification, because almost nothing eats only one thing.

teaches.heading: Chains, levels, and which way the arrows point

Food web.definition: All the food chains in a community drawn together, showing every feeding relationship at once. The extra connections are what make an ecosystem able to absorb damage.

teaches.heading: Chains, levels, and which way the arrows point

Interspecific.definition: Between different species. Interspecific competition is two different species needing the same resource, such as ants and grasshoppers both eating mesquite.

teaches.heading: Two kinds of limiting factor

Interspecific competition.definition: Competition between members of different species for the same limited resource. It shapes which species can live alongside one another.

teaches.heading: A real web: the Sonoran Desert

Intraspecific.definition: Within one species. Intraspecific competition is between members of the same species, and it is usually the fiercest kind because they need exactly the same things.

teaches.heading: Two kinds of limiting factor

Intraspecific competition.definition: Competition between members of the same species for the same limited resource. It is the main density-dependent force that produces an S-shaped growth curve.

teaches.heading: A real web: the Sonoran Desert

Invasive species.definition: An organism introduced by people into a habitat where it is not native, which then spreads at the expense of the native community. It succeeds largely because the predators and diseases that controlled it back home are absent.

teaches.heading: Learning targets for the unit

J-curve.definition: The shape exponential growth makes on ordinary axes — a long flat stretch, then a bend, then a near-vertical climb. The flat part is misleading: nothing has slowed down there.

teaches.heading: The J-curve, and the trick for reading it

Keystone species.definition: A species whose effect on its community is far larger than its abundance would suggest. Remove it and the whole structure changes, the way an arch falls when its keystone is taken out.

teaches.heading: Paine's crowbar, and the idea it produced

Lichens.definition: A fungus and an alga living together as a single organism. Lichens can grow on bare rock because the alga makes food and the fungus grips the rock and dissolves minerals out of it, which is why they are usually the first thing to colonise new ground.

teaches.heading: Primary and secondary succession

Limiting factor.definition: Anything that stops a population growing any further — food, water, space, predators, disease, weather. Limiting factors are what turn a J-curve into an S-curve.

teaches.heading: Two kinds of limiting factor

Logistic growth.definition: Growth that starts out exponential, then slows as the population approaches its carrying capacity, and finally levels off. It draws an S-shaped curve, and it is steepest halfway up.

teaches.heading: Learning targets for the unit

Organism.definition: One individual living thing — a single impala, a single bacterium, a single cactus.

teaches.heading: Learning targets for the unit

Overshoot.definition: When a population grows past its carrying capacity before the shortage of resources registers. It requires a delay in the feedback, and it is usually followed by a crash — and sometimes by a permanent drop in the carrying capacity itself.

teaches.heading: Overshoot, and the reindeer

Percent change.definition: How much a quantity grew or shrank between two times, worked out as (P2 minus P1) divided by P1, times 100. It tells you the total change end to end, not how fast the change happened.

teaches.heading: Percent change, and the thing it is not

Pioneer species.definition: The first organisms to colonise bare or cleared ground, such as lichens, mosses and fast-seeding weeds. They tolerate harsh conditions and disperse easily, but they are poor competitors and are soon replaced.

teaches.heading: Primary and secondary succession

Population.definition: A group of organisms of the same species living in the same area and able to breed with one another. It changes size only through births, deaths, immigration and emigration.

teaches.heading: A checklist for any population graph

Predation.definition: One organism hunting and eating another. It is a density-dependent factor, because predators find prey more easily and gather where prey is crowded.

teaches.heading: What exactly is growing

Primary succession.definition: Succession that starts on ground where there has never been soil, such as a new volcanic island or rock exposed by a retreating glacier. It is slow — often centuries — because the soil has to be manufactured first.

teaches.heading: Primary and secondary succession

Producer.definition: An organism that makes its own food from sunlight by photosynthesis, such as a plant or an alga. Producers are the first trophic level and the entry point for energy into a food web.

teaches.heading: The same two processes, at the scale of a landscape

Rate.definition: How much something changes per unit of time, such as 9.5 per cent per year. A rate is not the same as a percent change: the same total change can happen slowly or catastrophically fast.

teaches.heading: How you measure a rate you cannot see

Secondary succession.definition: Succession that starts on ground where the community was destroyed but the soil survived, such as after a fire or on abandoned farmland. It is much faster than primary succession because the soil and its seed bank are already there.

teaches.heading: Primary and secondary succession

Seral stage.definition: One of the intermediate communities a site passes through during succession, on the way to a climax community.

teaches.heading: Seral stages, climax communities, and an honest caveat

Trophic cascade.definition: A change at one level of a food web that spreads through the other levels, changing populations that were never touched directly. Removing a predator, for example, can end up changing which plants grow.

teaches.heading: Build the web, then break it

Trophic level.definition: An organism's position in a food web, counted in steps from the sunlight: producers are level one, herbivores level two, and so on. Only about a tenth of the energy at one level reaches the next.

teaches.heading: Chains, webs and trophic levels

Adaptation.definition: A heritable trait that raises an organism’s chance of surviving and reproducing in its environment. It is a property of a population produced by selection, not something an individual develops during its life.

teaches.heading: Adaptation and selection pressure

Adaptive radiation.definition: The rapid diversification of one ancestral lineage into many species, each occupying a different niche, typically after reaching new habitat or after a mass extinction frees up niches.

teaches.heading: Where we have got to

Allopatric speciation.definition: Speciation that begins with a geographic barrier physically separating two parts of a population, so gene flow between them stops.

teaches.heading: How one species becomes two

Analogous structure.definition: A structure shared by two species because they faced similar selection pressures, not because they inherited it from a common ancestor. Evidence of convergent evolution, not of ancestry.

teaches.heading: Line 2 — Comparative anatomy

Artificial selection.definition: Selective breeding by humans, who choose which individuals reproduce. The mechanism is the same as natural selection; only the source of the selection pressure differs.

teaches.heading: Natural and artificial selection

Biogeography.definition: The study of where species live and how they got there. Distribution patterns — such as related species clustered on neighbouring islands — are a line of evidence for common ancestry.

teaches.heading: Line 5 — Biogeography

Bottleneck effect.definition: A sharp reduction in population size that leaves the survivors with only a fraction of the original genetic variation, by chance rather than by fitness.

teaches.heading: Change without selection

Cladogram.definition: A branching diagram showing the most likely pattern of descent among a group of organisms. Each branch point represents a shared common ancestor, and shared derived characteristics determine where branches fall.

teaches.heading: Putting it together: reading a cladogram

Common ancestor.definition: A species from which two or more later species both descend. The more recently two species share one, the more characteristics they tend to share.

teaches.heading: How the five standards fit together

Convergent evolution.definition: Unrelated lineages independently evolving similar traits because they face similar selection pressures. Produces analogous structures.

teaches.heading: Where we have got to

Diffusion.definition: The net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration, as a result of their random motion.

teaches.heading: Diffusion

Directional selection.definition: Selection that favours one extreme of a trait, shifting the population mean towards it.

teaches.heading: Three patterns of selection

Disruptive selection.definition: Selection that favours both extremes of a trait over the intermediate, splitting a single distribution into two peaks.

teaches.heading: Where we have got to

Divergent evolution.definition: Related lineages accumulating differences over time as they adapt to different conditions. Produces homologous structures.

teaches.heading: Convergent and divergent evolution

Fitness.definition: An organism’s reproductive success relative to others in its population — how many surviving offspring it leaves, not how strong or fast it is.

teaches.heading: What an investigation actually is

Fossil record.definition: The total collection of preserved remains and traces of past life. Its ordering in rock layers shows which forms existed when, and documents transitions between groups.

teaches.heading: Line 1 — The fossil record

Founder effect.definition: The loss of genetic variation that happens when a small group leaves a population to found a new one, carrying only a sample of the original variation.

teaches.heading: The unit, lesson by lesson

Gene flow.definition: The movement of alleles between populations when individuals or gametes migrate and breed. It makes populations more genetically similar and works against speciation.

teaches.heading: The unit, lesson by lesson

Gene pool.definition: All the alleles present in all the individuals of a population.

teaches.heading: What exactly is growing

Genetic drift.definition: Change in allele frequencies from generation to generation due to chance alone. Its effects are strongest in small populations.

teaches.heading: The unit, lesson by lesson

Homologous structure.definition: A structure shared by two species because both inherited it from a common ancestor, even where it now performs different functions. Evidence of common ancestry.

teaches.heading: Line 2 — Comparative anatomy

HOX genes.definition: A family of genes that control the body plan of an embryo along the head-to-tail axis. They are remarkably similar across very different animals, which is evidence of shared ancestry.

teaches.heading: Line 3 — Embryological development

Microevolution.definition: Change in allele frequencies within a population over a small number of generations — evolution observable on a human timescale.

teaches.heading: Where we have got to

Natural selection.definition: The process by which individuals with heritable traits better suited to their environment survive and reproduce more than others, so those traits become more common in the population over generations.

teaches.heading: Is it actually natural selection?

Osmosis.definition: The net movement of water across a partially permeable membrane, from a solution with a lower solute concentration to a solution with a higher solute concentration.

teaches.heading: Osmosis

Phospholipid bilayer.definition: Two sheets of phospholipid molecules arranged tail to tail. It is the basic structure of every cell membrane.

teaches.heading: How the three standards fit together

Phylogeny.definition: The evolutionary history of a group of organisms — the pattern of who descended from whom.

teaches.heading: Putting it together: reading a cladogram

Postzygotic barrier.definition: A reproductive barrier acting after fertilisation, such as hybrid inviability or hybrid sterility, that prevents two populations from producing fertile offspring.

teaches.heading: What is a species?

Prezygotic barrier.definition: A reproductive barrier acting before fertilisation — differences in timing, behaviour, habitat, anatomy or gamete compatibility that stop mating or fertilisation happening at all.

teaches.heading: What is a species?

Selection pressure.definition: Any feature of the environment — a predator, a drought, an antibiotic — that causes some variants to survive and reproduce better than others.

teaches.heading: Adaptation and selection pressure

Speciation.definition: The process by which one population becomes two populations that can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring.

teaches.heading: Learning targets for the unit

Species.definition: A group of organisms that can interbreed in nature to produce fertile offspring. The definition is useful but imperfect — it is hard to apply to fossils, to asexual organisms, and to populations that hybridise.

teaches.heading: Species in the wrong place

Stabilizing selection.definition: Selection that favours the intermediate form of a trait over both extremes, narrowing the distribution around the existing mean.

teaches.heading: Three patterns of selection

Sympatric speciation.definition: Speciation without geographic separation — populations in the same place stop interbreeding for reasons such as a shift in host, timing or habitat preference.

teaches.heading: Where we have got to

Tonicity.definition: A comparison of solute concentration between a cell and the solution around it, which determines the direction of net water movement.

teaches.heading: How the three standards fit together

Vestigial structure.definition: A reduced structure that has lost most or all of its original function, retained from an ancestor in which it was functional.

teaches.heading: Before you start

Allele.definition: One of the alternative versions of a gene. An organism carries two alleles for each gene, one from each parent, and they may be the same or different.

teaches.heading: Multiple alleles — more than two versions

Anticodon.definition: The three-base sequence on a tRNA molecule that pairs with a matching codon on mRNA, so the correct amino acid is delivered to the ribosome.

teaches.heading: RNA — the working copy

Antiparallel.definition: Describing the two strands of a DNA molecule, which run in opposite directions to one another.

teaches.heading: Why the bases pair the way they do

Autosomal recessive.definition: An inheritance pattern in which the gene sits on a non-sex chromosome and two non-working copies are needed for the condition to appear. Carriers, with one copy, are unaffected.

teaches.heading: How two healthy parents have a child with CF

Carrier.definition: An individual who carries one copy of a recessive allele without showing the trait, and who can pass that allele on.

teaches.heading: Membrane structure

Central dogma.definition: The one-way flow of genetic information in a cell: DNA is transcribed into RNA, and RNA is translated into protein.

teaches.heading: The central dogma

Coding strand.definition: The DNA strand that is not read during transcription. Its sequence matches the finished mRNA, apart from having T wherever the RNA has U, which makes it a useful way to check your own transcription.

teaches.heading: Transcription — writing the message

Crossing over.definition: The swapping of matching segments between homologous chromosomes during meiosis. It produces chromosomes carrying combinations of alleles that have never sat together before.

teaches.heading: Source one: crossing over

Independent assortment.definition: The separation of each pair of chromosomes during meiosis without regard to any other pair, so the allele a gamete receives for one gene says nothing about which it receives for another.

teaches.heading: Source two: independent assortment

Retrovirus.definition: A virus, such as HIV, that stores its genes as RNA and carries reverse transcriptase, allowing it to write a DNA copy of itself into the DNA of the cell it infects.

teaches.heading: Learning targets for the unit

Reverse transcriptase.definition: A viral enzyme that builds DNA from an RNA template — transcription in reverse. Human cells do not have one, which is why the central dogma runs only one way in them.

teaches.heading: Case study — how an mRNA vaccine works

Codon.definition: A group of three consecutive bases in mRNA that specifies one amino acid, or signals translation to stop.

teaches.heading: What you will actually do

Cystic fibrosis.definition: An autosomal recessive condition caused by two non-working copies of the CFTR gene. Without working CFTR protein, cells cannot move chloride properly and mucus becomes thick and sticky.

teaches.heading: Cystic fibrosis, from the gene outwards

Dihybrid cross.definition: A cross that follows two genes at once. Two parents heterozygous for both genes give a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 phenotype ratio.

teaches.heading: What you will actually do

DNA.definition: Deoxyribonucleic acid, the nucleic acid that carries an organism’s genetic instructions. Two strands of nucleotides twist into a double helix, held together by bases paired A–T and G–C, and the order of the bases is the code.

teaches.heading: DNA, gene, chromosome — three words, one object

DNA replication.definition: The copying of a DNA molecule. The strands separate and each acts as a template for a new partner strand.

teaches.heading: Why the two gametes are built so differently

Dominant.definition: An allele expressed in the phenotype whenever it is present, even as a single copy. Dominant does not mean common, strong or better.

teaches.heading: The equation, and everything it hides

Gene.definition: A stretch of DNA that codes for one protein. A gene is a section of a chromosome, not a separate object attached to it.

teaches.heading: Gene expression: which instructions are being followed

Genotype.definition: The combination of alleles an organism carries for a gene, such as Aa. Two organisms with different genotypes can share a phenotype.

teaches.heading: The part the genotype does not decide

Heterozygous.definition: Having two different alleles for a gene, such as Aa.

teaches.heading: Learning targets for the unit

Homozygous.definition: Having two identical alleles for a gene, such as AA or aa.

teaches.heading: Learning targets for the unit

Hydrogen bond.definition: A weak attraction that, in DNA, holds paired bases together. An A–T pair shares two; a G–C pair shares three, making it the stronger pair.

teaches.heading: Why the bases pair the way they do

Mutation.definition: A change in a DNA sequence. Mutations may be harmful, harmless or beneficial — which one depends on where the change falls and what the organism is doing with that protein.

teaches.heading: What a mutation actually is

Nucleic acid.definition: A macromolecule built from a chain of nucleotides. DNA and RNA are the two nucleic acids.

teaches.heading: Learning targets for the unit

Nucleotide.definition: The repeating unit of a nucleic acid, made of a phosphate group, a sugar and a nitrogenous base.

teaches.heading: Four families, one design idea

Pedigree.definition: A diagram of a family across several generations, used to work out how a trait is inherited and to infer genotypes from the phenotypes you can see.

teaches.heading: Learning targets for the unit

Phenotype.definition: The observable characteristics of an organism, produced by its genotype together with its environment.

teaches.heading: Learning targets for the unit

Polygenic.definition: Describing a trait controlled by many genes acting together, giving a continuous range of phenotypes rather than distinct categories. Height and skin colour are polygenic.

teaches.heading: Polygenic inheritance — and why you are not a pea

Punnett square.definition: A grid used to find the possible allele combinations in offspring, and so the probability of each genotype and phenotype. It gives a chance for each offspring, not a quota.

teaches.heading: Learning targets for the unit

Recessive.definition: An allele expressed in the phenotype only when two copies are present, because a single dominant allele would mask it.

teaches.heading: Learning targets for the unit

RNA.definition: A single-stranded nucleic acid that uses the sugar ribose and the base uracil in place of thymine. mRNA carries the message, tRNA delivers amino acids, and rRNA forms part of the ribosome.

teaches.heading: RNA — the working copy

Semiconservative.definition: Describing DNA replication, in which each new molecule keeps one original strand and gains one newly built strand.

teaches.heading: Replication: copying the molecule

Template.definition: A strand used as the pattern for building a matching strand. Because base pairing is fixed, the template determines its partner’s sequence completely.

teaches.heading: Why the bases pair the way they do

Template strand.definition: The strand of DNA that RNA polymerase reads during transcription, and against which the mRNA is built.

teaches.heading: Transcription — writing the message

Trait.definition: An observable characteristic of an organism, such as flower colour or blood group.

teaches.heading: Primary and secondary succession

Transcription.definition: The making of an RNA copy of a gene, carried out by RNA polymerase inside the nucleus.

teaches.heading: Transcription — writing the message

Translation.definition: The building of a protein from an mRNA message, carried out by a ribosome in the cytoplasm, reading three bases at a time.

teaches.heading: Translation — reading the message
